Chapter 2: The Awakening of Curiosity and the Power of Books
As childhood faded and the teenage years began, the world just seemed to get bigger, didn’t it? Sure, the routines at home and school were still there, but something inside was shifting. The girl who used to accept every rule without a second thought now felt a spark—a curiosity—drawing her toward the unknown. She craved answers, especially the ones no one around her seemed willing to give.
Books became more than just a way to pass the time. They turned into a lifeline. Every novel, every essay opened the door to new lives, new ideas—ideas that sometimes shook the very foundation of what she’d always believed. Reading wasn’t just for fun anymore; it was a way to break out of the tight boundaries of her upbringing and dream about what else might be possible.
The family’s apartment, with all its careful trappings of respectability, slowly became the backdrop for quiet acts of rebellion. While her mother busied herself with chores and her father reminisced about old regrets, the girl would slip away to her room, book in hand. There, she read about distant places, bold women, and men who dared to question authority. Every story showed her a different kind of world—one where people actually made their own choices, free from everyone else’s expectations.
Even school started to look different. The lessons were still strict and structured, but she started to notice things she hadn’t before. Teachers who once seemed so wise now appeared limited—their knowledge carefully boxed in by what was safe, what was acceptable. She saw the gaps in their explanations, how they dodged the tough questions. Suddenly, it was clear: if she wanted real understanding, it wouldn’t come from just following the rules. It would come from questioning them.
Friendships began to matter in a whole new way. Some classmates shared her curiosity, eager to dig deeper. Others clung to what they knew, comforted by tradition. Conversations got heavier—touching on politics, religion, and what it really meant to be a woman. For the first time, she realized she wasn’t alone in her doubts. There were others who felt that same restless urge to break free.
At home, though, things got tense. Her mother, sensing the change, doubled down on the rules. She worried about the influence of books, and about the risks of too much independence. Her father, caught somewhere between pride and fear, encouraged her to aim high—but always warned her not to stray too far from what was expected. The girl felt torn—pulled between the comfort of family and the thrill of discovery.
And it wasn’t just her mind that was struggling. Emotionally, it was a real tug-of-war. Sometimes she felt guilty, wondering if her curiosity meant she was betraying her family. Other times, she was exhilarated—like when a new idea made the world suddenly feel brighter and more alive. Questioning things wasn’t easy, but it was impossible to stop.
Little by little, the walls of her world started to shift. Things that once seemed absolutely certain—her parents’ authority, society’s rules, what she was supposed to be as a girl—all of it now felt open to challenge. She realized that becoming an adult wasn’t just about getting older. It was about deciding which values to hold onto, and which ones to let go.
Alone in her room, surrounded by books, she began to dream of a different future. One that wouldn’t always be easy, or make everyone happy. But the chance to live authentically—to make her own choices—was just too powerful to ignore.
This awakening of curiosity wasn’t a sudden jolt. It was a slow, unfolding process. Each new idea, every deep conversation, all those small acts of defiance—they added up. And with each step, the world felt bigger, more complicated, and full of promise.
